title: Why an AI Builder Should Leave Blanks
metaDescription: An invented phone number belongs to a real stranger. Why Kodely writes a bracketed placeholder instead of a plausible fact about your business.
targetKeyword: ai website builder makes up information
body: Give an AI website builder one line about your business and it will hand back a finished-looking page. Somewhere on that page there will usually be an address, a phone number, a set of opening hours, and three warm testimonials from people with first names and last initials.
None of it is true. All of it looks true. That combination is the problem.
The failure is not "it wrote something wrong"

Language models fill gaps. That is close to what they are for. Ask for a website for a plumber in Leeds and the model has seen thousands of plumbers' websites, so it knows the shape: a number in the header, hours in the footer, a review that says the engineer was punctual and tidied up afterwards. Producing that shape is not a malfunction.
It becomes one the moment the page goes on a real business's real domain. Then:

• An invented phone number is somebody's actual phone number. Someone with a burst pipe rings a stranger.
  • Invented opening hours send a real customer to a locked door on a Sunday.
  • An invented testimonial is a fabricated endorsement attributed to a person who does not exist — a thing with legal weight in most advertising regimes, not just a taste problem.
  • An invented price is one you either honour or explain away.
And the reason these survive to publication is precisely that they look right. Nobody proofreads a plausible detail. You proofread the heading you did not like.
What Kodely does instead

The builder is instructed never to fabricate a fact about a real business: no street addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, opening hours, prices, staff names, years in business, customer counts, awards, certifications, review scores or testimonials.
Where it does not know one, it writes a clearly bracketed placeholder — [your phone number], [your address], [your opening hours] — and moves on.

A bracket is deliberately ugly. It is an obvious instruction to fill something in, visible from across the room in a preview, and impossible to publish by accident without noticing. A plausible-looking invention is the opposite: it is designed, by its nature, to be overlooked.
This deliberately overrides "no placeholder text"
There is a tension here worth naming, because it is the interesting part.

Generated sites are also told, firmly, never to ship Lorem ipsum or headings that say "Your Title Here". Placeholder copy is what makes an AI-built page feel like a draft rather than a site, and it is one of the main reasons generated pages read as generic.

So the two rules pull against each other, and the ordering matters: not knowing a fact does not license inventing one. Invent freely where invention is a design decision — headlines, section copy, taglines, colour, layout, the visual idea of the page. Never where it is a claim about the world.
What this means for your prompt

It means the facts you supply are the facts you get, so bring them. A prompt with your real service list, real hours and real prices produces a page you can publish. A prompt without them produces a page with brackets in it, which is a to-do list rather than a failure.
Two things worth doing:

• Paste real quotes if you want testimonials. Write the words you want on the page. Do not ask for testimonials and let the model write them — whatever comes back is an endorsement nobody gave you.
  • Give the destination, not the intent. "A booking button" gets a bracketed link. "A booking button linking to [your real booking URL]" gets a working one.

If writing all that out feels like effort, type one line and press Enhance. It expands your idea into a fuller brief you read and edit before building, with brackets where real-world facts belong — and it costs no credits, because a preview of what you are about to spend on should not itself cost anything.
The test for any builder
If you are evaluating AI website tools, this is a cheap and revealing thing to check. Describe a business, deliberately omit the phone number and the hours, and look at what comes back.
If there is a phone number on the page, the tool made it up, and it will make up other things you are less likely to catch.
Try it with 750 free credits — bring your real details and see how much of the page you can publish unedited. See also: how to write a prompt that gets a good first build.
